transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-08 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CascadeAI Head of ML), Evan Ross (Platform), Samir Patel (CTO)

Summary: quick demo of Redwood Evaluate / Quality monitoring: prompt sets, regression alerts, A/B comparison flows in Console and via API.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining — excited to walk through the eval and quality monitoring capabilities, should be about 40 minutes, we'll leave time for q's. priya, samir, evan, thanks for taking the time.
[00:10] Priya (CascadeAI): thanks maya, hi liam. quick context: we have a internal inference pipeline, running a mix of open models and a few in-house fine-tuned variants. main ask is automated regression detection when we change models or prompts, and a straightforward A/B flow to compare variants.
[00:25] Liam (Redwood SE): great, that's exactly what this is for. quick agenda: prompt-set management, metrics we capture, how alerts are configured, and demo of the A/B comparison workflow in the Console and via the API/Optimize.
[00:40] Maya: just to call out constraints you mentioned earlier priya — latency targets ~250ms p50 for NLU routes, and strict PII retention policies. we can cover how Private/Dedicated options map there but today focus on the eval product.
[01:05] Priya: perfect. also curious about how you handle prompt canonicalization — we have variable user context and want canonical prompts for apples-to-apples comparisons.
[01:20] Liam: yeah, good question. in the Console we support prompt-set definitions where you can include template variables and a canonicalizer step. it's a lightweight transform — strip session ids, normalize timestamps, mask PHI tokens — that runs before eval. we've found customers call it different names so sometimes the auto-transcribe says "kay-vee cache" instead of KV cache, so you'll see some weirdness in the logs, but the canonicalizer helps.
[01:50] Evan (CascadeAI): does that run client-side or in Redwood? any PII concerns?
[01:55] Liam: runs as part of the eval pipeline on Redwood's processing layer; for Private customers it can run inside your VPC. we also support a pre-processing webhook so you can canonicalize on your side and send canonical prompts to Redwood.
[02:25] Samir (CTO): what's the signal suite? like how do you define regressions beyond simple loss metrics?
[02:35] Liam: good one — we capture a set of automated metrics: semantic similarity to references (embedding cosine distributions), exact match rates, hallucination indicators (model-assert confidence vs ground-truth), length divergence, and a custom rubric scoring system where you can upload human labels and we compute recall/precision-like metrics. we also compute delta distributions and look for shifts with statistical tests — e.g., KS test on similarity scores — to detect regressions.
[03:10] Priya: do you support thresholded alerts? we want to be notified if a metric drops by more than X% or falls below an absolute threshold.
[03:18] Maya: yep. in Alerts you can set absolute thresholds, relative deltas, and rolling-window regressions. alerts can trigger Slack, PagerDuty, or a webhook with the failing sample set and a link into the Console.
[03:35] Evan: nice. in terms of sampling, if an alert fires, does Redwood give you the full failing examples with context and model outputs?
[03:42] Liam: yes, the alert payload includes N example traces (configurable), the prompt, model response, reference, the metric values, and links to the trace in Console. you can also include pre/post-canonicalized prompts in the payload.
[04:00] Priya: show us the Console?
[04:05] Maya: sure i'm sharing my screen — ok this is the Eval workspace. on the left you see prompt-sets, at top you can create a new set or import CSVs.
[04:25] Liam: here's a prompt-set we created for a support triage workflow — note the columns: user_query, context_snippet, expected_label. you can add variants and tags (smoke/regression/edge).
[04:40] Priya: can we attach a canonicalization rule?
[04:45] Liam: yes, this rule: regex replacement for order ids, mask emails, normalize timestamps. you can preview canonicalization on the right — sometimes the preview shows odd tokenization, like it might mark "V-P-C" in the transcript instead of VPC because of ASR outputs, but that's fine.
[05:10] Maya: moving to metrics dashboard — top-left shows overall pass rate, average similarity, and a hallucination score. underneath is a histogram of similarity scores so you can see distribution shifts over time.
[05:30] Priya: what does hallucination score mean here?
[05:33] Liam: it's an aggregate that combines divergence from reference, presence of facts contradicted by the reference, and a model confidence mismatch. it's configurable — you can weight the components.
[05:50] Samir: are the weights versioned with the prompt-set so our teams can reproduce prior evals?
[05:56] Liam: yes, everything's versioned. prompt-set versions, canonicalization rules, metric configs, and model pinning. when you run an A/B test we snapshot the full config.
[06:10] Priya: show A/B comparison flow.
[06:15] Liam: sure — create a test, pick baseline model and variant, choose metric(s) — here we pick similarity and hallucination — and launch. you can run sync (one-off batch) or stream (real-time). for your PV we recommend a sync batch first to get baseline numbers.
[06:40] Maya: I'll trigger a demo run using two models: open-1-large (baseline) and redwood-ft-qa-1 (variant). starting run now — this will take a minute to compute aggregates.
[06:55] [07:10] System: run started, 1200 samples queued.
[07:15] Priya: 1200 samples — that's similar to our pilot size. how do you handle sampling bias?
[07:22] Liam: you can stratify by tags, user cohorts, or source traffic. we also provide helper scripts in the API to sample uniformly across user buckets.
[07:40] [08:00] Maya: results are in — on the right you can see comparative metrics and a significance test. similarity delta is -1.8% for variant, hallucination +0.6%. the significance test flags similarity as not significant at p<0.05, but hallucination is marginal.
[08:30] Priya: interesting — can we look at failing examples?
[08:35] Liam: click 'Failed examples' — here's one. original prompt, canonicalized prompt, baseline response, variant response, reference. you can add an annotation and assign to a reviewer.
[08:55] Evan: if we annotate a sample as "bad", will that feed back into the model ops? like retrain signals?
[09:03] Liam: annotations are stored and can be exported. Redwood doesn't retrain models for you but we integrate with training pipelines — you can export labeled sets to S3 for your training job. we also have a rules engine to auto-route high-severity failures into a retraining bucket.
[09:25] Priya: what about realtime A/B rollouts — can we do gradual traffic splits and automatic rollbacks on regression?
[09:33] Maya: yes — Optimize has traffic routing policies. you can configure a canary with X% traffic, monitor metrics, and set automatic rollback if the chosen metric degrades beyond a threshold. that works for Hosted and Dedicated; for Private we recommend a similar control plane policy.
[09:53] Samir: how do the regression alerts look for canary? we need no false positives.
[09:59] Liam: for canary we compute both absolute and relative metrics across windows and use bootstrapped CIs to avoid noisy signals; you can choose sensitivity. also option to require sustained regression across multiple windows before triggering rollback.
[10:20] Priya: about integrations: our monitoring stack is Datadog and Slack. can alerts go into Datadog?
[10:26] Liam: yes we have native Datadog metrics export and you can send alerts via webhook to Datadog or Slack. Payload includes sample IDs so you can cross-link.
[10:40] Priya: latency — if we run these evals against rolled out traffic, does evaling add overhead?
[10:45] Maya: for inline evals we recommend sampling 1-5% of traffic to avoid added p99s; we also support async tracing where we log request/response for background batch evals.
[11:05] Evan: curious about cost — running heavy similarity embedding comparisons for 1200 samples, what's the unit cost?
[11:10] Liam: cost depends on whether you run on Hosted vs Dedicated. for small pilots we can estimate the compute cost; Optimize will recommend a quantization/profile setting to drop costs — e.g., run similarity embeddings on a quantized embedding model to reduce GPU cost. we'll include a cost estimate in the pilot pricing.
[11:35] Priya: instruments and metrics — can we add custom metrics? we want a "policy-violation" metric detected by heuristics.
[11:43] Liam: yep you can define custom metrics via API or upload a scoring script. the console will run it inside a sandboxed container at eval-time. the script returns a numeric score per sample.
[12:00] Priya: that sandbox — is that in our VPC for private deployments?
[12:05] Liam: for Private yes; for hosted it's sandboxed in Redwood environment with restrictions and an audit trail.
[12:18] Maya: quick note on reproducibility — every run gets a run_id. you can reproduce by passing run_id to the API or re-running the same snapshot.
[12:30] Priya: any limitations on dataset size?
[12:33] Liam: for very large runs we recommend batch jobs to S3 and then run a job that reads from S3; Console handles up to millions of samples via batch. interactive runs are sized for up to 5k samples comfortably.
[12:50] Samir: what about privacy — do you retain raw prompts?
[12:54] Maya: default retention is 90 days for hosted, configurable; for enterprise you can set shorter retention and ensure no raw prompt logs are stored by using client-side canonicalization or Private deployment. we also support KMS/HSM for keys.
[13:15] Evan: can we run this with our Dedicated capacity?
[13:18] Maya: yes, Dedicated works fine. it gives you predictable throughput and your data stays in your tenancy. the Eval control-plane still gives you the Console experience.
[13:30] Priya: API demo of creating a prompt-set?
[13:33] Liam: sure — here's a cURL example: POST /v1/evals/promptsets with CSV URL and config body. you'll get back prompt_set_id. then POST /v1/evals/runs with model variants and metrics. there's also an SDK snippet.
[14:00] Priya: can we programmatically attach canonicalization rules?
[14:04] Liam: yes via the API or via the Console YAML export/import.
[14:20] Priya: sample comparator workbook — will you provide an example for A/B reporting?
[14:25] Maya: yes we'll share a spreadsheet that captures metric deltas, significance, sample examples, and recommended actions.
[14:40] Evan: security docs?
[14:42] Maya: will send SOC2 pack, network architecture, and data flow diagrams.
[14:50] Priya: two concerns: 1) our operations team wants deterministic reproducible runs and 2) avoid noisy auto-rollbacks. both seem addressable.
[15:00] Liam: totally — reproducibility via snapshots/run_ids and conservative rollback settings. you can test with a 1% canary then scale.
[15:12] Priya: how do you handle prompt drift over time? we see production prompts change wording.
[15:18] Liam: we have drift detection on embedding space and language distribution. triggers can create a backlog for human review. you can pipe drifted samples into a retrain bucket.
[15:35] Priya: what about A/B comparison visualization exports?
[15:38] Liam: exportable CSV or PDF reports; also an API endpoint to pull the aggregated stats.
[15:50] Maya: ok last piece — running continuous monitoring vs scheduled runs.
[15:55] Liam: set up a recurring eval job daily/weekly, or enable streaming where samples are evaluated as they come. streaming is heavier but gives near realtime detection.
[16:10] Samir: what's the onboarding timeline for a POC?
[16:14] Maya: usually 1-2 weeks to onboard, get sample prompt-sets in, and run baseline. pilot runs 2-4 weeks.
[16:25] Priya: what metrics should we prioritize?
[16:28] Liam: similarity + hallucination + domain-specific policy violations. start with a small prioritized prompt-set to reduce noise.
[16:38] Maya: recap and next steps: we'll send pricing & SOW, SOC2/security packet, sample prompt-set template and A/B workbook, schedule POC kickoff next week.
[16:50] Priya: sounds good, thanks for the demo.
[16:55] Samir: thanks, appreciate the thoroughness.
[17:00] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and calendar invite. bye.

End of transcript.
